idiom_name: typed gateway interface over fetch with an injected connection function
implementation_notes: TypeScript contributes the domestic interface as a type: declare the gateway as an interface of application-level operations and realise it as a module of async functions or a small class that holds the base URL and an injected connection (Fowler's BoneFusionGateway takes the connection in its constructor so a test can pass a stub). Requests still run over fetch (or undici in Node), and the gateway is the single place that checks res.ok, decodes into the domestic types and converts failures; putting a runtime validator (zod, io-ts, a type guard) at this seam makes a foreign payload that changed shape fail at the boundary instead of inside business code. Because the connection is a function, the seam is trivial to substitute - do not mock the global fetch.
pitfalls: Response.json() is typed any: casting it to a domestic interface re-introduces the foreign shape with a false sense of safety - validate at the gateway.
Keep the injected connection the only seam; mocking global fetch or a module couples tests to module resolution and hides missing translations.
Node and browser fetch differ in error semantics (network failures reject, 4xx/5xx resolve), and AbortSignal/timeout handling is caller-visible: the gateway must translate both consistently.
A class with a private connection plus a public interface is only worth it when methods share state; for one or two operations a module of functions is the smaller gateway.
